uncited: Hard Voxelization discretizes a continuous 3D point cloud into a fixed-size 3D grid of cubic voxels by binning points based on their spatial coordinates and aggregating associated attribute values within each voxel [S3, unofficial].
It solves the problem of converting unstructured point data into a regular grid structure suitable for convolutional neural networks or efficient spatial queries.
It differs from its siblings by enforcing a strict grid topology where points are assigned to specific voxels based on deterministic coordinate mapping, unlike probabilistic or sparse variants.
The grid dimensions are derived from the range and voxel size.
Points falling into the same voxel are aggregated.
Common strategies include storing all points up to a limit, averaging attributes, or computing a centroid.
Standard hard voxelization may rely on atomic operations which are non-deterministic.
Deterministic variants use explicit sorting or unique-coordinate identification to ensure reproducible output order [S3, unofficial].
Hard voxelization is a fundamental preprocessing step in 3D computer vision, particularly for LiDAR-based object detection and autonomous driving perception systems.
It was popularized by frameworks like MMDetection3D and PointPillars, which require regular grid inputs for 3D CNNs or 2D projection networks.
The method originated from the need to efficiently process sparse point clouds by converting them into dense voxel grids, allowing the use of standard convolutional operations.
